title: Trial and Error vs Systematic Investigation in SR&ED | Canada FAQ
description: In Canada's SR&ED program, random trial and error or unguided attempts until something works fail the CRA's "How" requirement.
summary: In Canada's SR&ED program, random trial-and-error or unguided attempts until something works fail the CRA's "How" requirement. Businesses in Canada claiming federal incentives must show a systematic investigation: a hypothesis consistent with known facts, controlled experiments or analysis, logical conclusions and contemporaneous records. Failed projects still qualify when this disciplined process is documented.

1. Executive Summary and the 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation
1.1 Evolution of the Federal SR&ED Architecture

Established in 1944 and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) in accordance with fiscal and tax policy formulated by the Department of Finance Canada, the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program represents the foundational pillar of federal industrial innovation support in Canada. Operating through the interlocking provisions of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"), the program delivers a dual-layered statutory incentive to taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada that perform scientific research or experimental development within Canadian jurisdiction. First, subsection 37(1) of the ITA enables claimants to aggregate qualifying current and restored capital SR&ED expenditures into a dedicated expenditure pool that may be deducted up to 100% against business income in the taxation year incurred or carried forward indefinitely to reduce taxable income in subsequent taxation years. Second, section 127 and section 127.1 of the ITA generate an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a general corporate rate of 15% to an enhanced refundable rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Between 2012 and 2024, federal legislative contractions had progressively narrowed the eligible cost base and credit generosity of the SR&ED regime. Over that twelve-year span, the statutory percentage used to calculate the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for notional overhead under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR was reduced from 65% for 2012 and prior years to 60% for 2013, and subsequently to 55% for 2014 and later taxation years. Concurrently, effective in 2014, depreciable capital property and equipment lease payments were eliminated from SR&ED expenditure and ITC eligibility, arm's-length contract payments and third-party payments were restricted to an 80% inclusion rate for ITC calculation purposes under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, and the general corporate ITC rate was set at 15%. While those restrictions curbed federal tax expenditures, macroeconomic outcomes over the ensuing decade revealed persistent structural challenges across the Canadian economy, including sluggish labour productivity growth, intense international competition for mobile research capital, internal trade barriers, and a pronounced "scale-up penalty" whereby Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) immediately forfeited access to the 35% refundable SR&ED tax credit upon listing their shares on a public stock exchange.
1.2 Chronology of the 2024–2026 Statutory Reforms and Bill C-15 Royal Assent

To reverse sluggish productivity growth and strengthen domestic intellectual property retention, the Department of Finance Canada executed a multi-year legislative overhaul of the SR&ED program between 2024 and 2026. Following an initial policy review announced in Federal Budget 2021, Federal Budget 2024 launched a second formal public consultation aimed at modernizing the SR&ED incentive framework without increasing the overall benchmark corporate income tax rate of 15%. The insights gathered during the Budget 2024 consultation directly shaped the policy package unveiled in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024. In that statement, the federal government proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million and $75 million respectively, extending eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restoring the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures for both the section 37 income deduction and the section 127 ITC components of the program.

On August 15, 2025, the Department of Finance Canada released comprehensive draft legislative proposals to amend the ITA and ITR, translating the 2024 Fall Economic Statement announcements into statutory text and inviting stakeholder technical submissions through September 12, 2025. Issued alongside technical amendments governing the Excessive Interest and Financing Expenses Limitation (EIFEL) exemptions, foreign affiliate dumping and Foreign Accrual Business Income (FABI) rules for CCPCs, the Global Minimum Tax (Pillar Two), and CRA compliance powers, the August 15, 2025 draft SR&ED legislation represented the most substantial structural expansion of Canada's R&D tax architecture in more than a decade. Because Parliament had experienced prorogation earlier in 2025 and the August 15, 2025 draft proposals had not yet been tabled as a bill in the House of Commons as at September 30, 2025, Canadian corporate financial statement preparers operating under IFRS Accounting Standards were initially precluded from treating the draft enhancements as substantively enacted for third-quarter 2025 deferred tax recognition.

Shortly thereafter, in Federal Budget 2025 (tabled in November 2025), the federal government reaffirmed its intention to enact the August 15, 2025 legislative package and introduced a major further expansion: increasing the annual expenditure limit on which the 35% enhanced SR&ED tax credit can be earned from the previously announced $4.5 million to $6.0 million. Made retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (the date of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), this $6.0 million expenditure limit doubled the maximum annual refundable federal cash credit for qualifying corporations from $1,050,000 under the pre-reform law to $2,100,000. The enacting legislation—Bill C-15 (the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3)—subsequently passed Parliament and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Upon Royal Assent, the CRA commenced a formal update of its SR&ED administrative policies and tax forms while advising claimants to continue submitting claims through standard electronic filing channels. Building upon the enacted Bill C-15 framework, Federal Budget 2026 announced an additional policy proposal to expand the SR&ED regime to cover certain commercialization activities and costs (regulatory and certification testing directly related to an eligible SR&ED project, and the registration and maintenance of intellectual property protection) for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026, alongside a proposed extension of the Clean Electricity and Clean Technology Investment Tax Credits to property that becomes available for use before 2041.
1.3 Summary Comparison of Pre-Reform vs. Post-Reform Federal SR&ED Parameters

The transition from the pre-December 16, 2024 rules to the modernized regime enacted under Bill C-15 alters the after-tax cost of conducting R&D in Canada for both private scale-ups and publicly traded domestic technology enterprises. By replacing the balance-sheet taxable capital test with a three-year average revenue test for eligible Canadian public corporations and reinstating depreciable R&D equipment, the statutory framework eliminates the historical disincentive against domestic public listings and hardware-intensive experimentation.

body.text: 2. Statutory Framework and Legal Definitions Under the Income Tax Act
2.1 Subsection 248(1): The Tripartite Definition of Eligible SR&ED

The statutory foundation for all federal SR&ED claims—and for provincial R&D tax credits that harmonize with federal tax law—resides in the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that encompasses three distinct categories of core scientific or technological work. The first category, codified in paragraph 248(1)(a), is basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically occurs in foundational scientific inquiries where investigators seek to uncover physical laws, biological mechanisms, or theoretical properties without targeting an immediate commercial product. The second category, codified in paragraph 248(1)(b), is applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research bridges pure theory and industrial deployment by directing rigorous scientific inquiry toward a defined functional objective.

The third and commercially predominant category, codified in paragraph 248(1)(c), is experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Across Canadian industry—spanning software engineering, advanced manufacturing, clean technology, chemical processing, and industrial product design—experimental development accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims. Crucially, the statutory phrase "including incremental improvements thereto" confirms that a taxpayer need not invent a disruptive, first-in-the-world product to qualify; evolutionary enhancements to existing proprietary processes, materials, or software architectures satisfy paragraph 248(1)(c) provided they are undertaken to resolve genuine technological uncertainty and generate new technological knowledge that was not achievable through standard practice.
2.2 Eligible Support Work vs. Statutory Exclusions

Beyond core basic research, applied research, and experimental development, paragraph 248(1)(d) of the ITA extends SR&ED eligibility to specific categories of support work—namely, work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. In CRA administrative practice and Tax Court jurisprudence, support work possesses no independent eligibility; it can never qualify as SR&ED on its own, but instead rides on the back of a qualifying core project under paragraph (a), (b), or (c). If no qualifying core project exists, no support work can be claimed.

Furthermore, the CRA draws the legal boundary between eligible support work and statutorily excluded commercial activities by examining the underlying purpose for which the activity was performed. Under subsection 248(1), routine data collection, quality control, routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, market research, sales promotion, style or aesthetic modifications, and commercial production are expressly excluded from SR&ED. As illustrated by the CRA's administrative guidance, if data collection, computer programming, or physical testing is carried out to support normal business operations, customer feature requests, or production quality assurance, it is excluded. Conversely, if that exact same category of data collection, programming, or testing is commensurate with the technical needs of, and carried out for the direct purpose of supporting, an active experimental investigation aimed at resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d).
2.3 Section 37 Deduction Pool and Section 127 Investment Tax Credit Mechanics

The financial architecture of an SR&ED claim operates through two separate but interconnected statutory accounts in the ITA: the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Section 37 and the Investment Tax Credit calculation on Qualified Expenditures under Section 127. Under subsection 37(1) (specifically paragraph 37(1)(a) for current expenditures and the restored capital provisions for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024), a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada aggregates its domestic SR&ED expenditures (plus permissible foreign employee wages under subsection 37(1.5)) into a cumulative deductible pool. Canadian tax law allows a taxpayer to deduct up to 100% of its positive section 37 pool balance in the current taxation year or carry any unclaimed balance forward indefinitely to future taxation years. Where a corporation undergoes an amalgamation or winding-up, its tax attributes generally flow through under continuity rules, whereas following an acquisition of control, carryforward balances remain deductible only if the corporation continues to carry on the same or a similar business.

In parallel, subsection 127(9) of the ITA defines the "qualified expenditures" upon which the 15% or 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is calculated. Tax auditors and corporate controllers must carefully reconcile three structural divergences between the section 37 deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base. First, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA, the resulting Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—calculated at 55% of the directly engaged SR&ED salary base under Regulation 2900(4)—is included in "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) to earn the ITC, but the PPA is never added to the section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool; instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA stands in for are deducted under general business income principles pursuant to subsection 9(1) of the ITA. Second, whereas 100% of an eligible arm's-length SR&ED contract payment or third-party payment enters the section 37 deductible pool, subsection 127(9) restricts the amount included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes to 80% of the eligible payment. Third, certain expenditures that pass the general income deduction test—such as SR&ED claim preparation fees, attendance at general scientific conferences, and certain financing costs—are barred by section 2902 of the ITR and subsection 127(9) of the ITA from earning any ITC.
2.4 Recapture Rules and Paragraph 12(1)(t) Subsequent-Year Income Inclusion

A critical accounting reality of the Canadian SR&ED regime is that the section 37 deduction and the section 127 ITC are not independent, tax-free subsidies; rather, the federal ITC claimed in one taxation year is subject to statutory recovery in the immediately following taxation year. Under paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in Year 1 (whether applied to offset Part I tax payable or received as a refundable cash payment) must first be deducted from the taxpayer's section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in Year 2. When a taxpayer has claimed its full section 37 deduction in Year 1, deducting the Year 1 ITC from the pool in Year 2 drives the pool negative, and that negative balance is mandatorily included in the taxpayer's taxable business income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(t). As a result, an engineering firm, manufacturer, or product design studio that budgets the gross cash refund without reserving for the following taxation year's paragraph 12(1)(t) corporate income tax inclusion will experience an unanticipated tax liability in Year 2.

In addition to the annual paragraph 12(1)(t) income inclusion, the ITA enforces ITC recapture rules whenever property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned—such as materials transformed into an experimental prototype or test unit, or restored depreciable capital equipment acquired on or after December 16, 2024—is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use. Upon disposition or conversion to commercial use, the recaptured portion of the previously claimed ITC is added directly back to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion, preventing taxpayers from using SR&ED tax credits to subsidize the cost of commercial inventory or commercial production machinery.
3. Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Out Mechanics, and Refundability
3.1 The Enhanced 35% Credit Rate and Expansion to Canadian Public Corporations

Under the modernized SR&ED framework effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026), qualifying corporations earn an enhanced SR&ED ITC rate of 35% on qualified expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit of $6,000,000. Prior to this reform, eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate was restricted exclusively to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), which also benefit from the federal small-business deduction on up to $500,000 of active business income. Under the pre-reform rules, any Canadian technology or life-sciences company that accessed public equity markets via an initial public offering (IPO) ceased to be a CCPC and immediately saw its SR&ED credit rate drop from 35% refundable to 15% non-refundable.

Recognizing that this structural cliff discouraged domestic public listings and constrained capital formation for mid-sized innovators, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the August 15, 2025 draft legislation, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15 extended the 35% enhanced refundable SR&ED tax credit to eligible Canadian public corporations for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Consequently, both qualifying CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations now share access to the same 35% enhanced credit rate and the same $6,000,000 maximum annual expenditure limit.
3.2 Mathematical Mechanics of the $6.0 Million Expenditure Limit Phase-Out

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual SR&ED Expenditure Limit is $6,000,000, representing a doubling of the legacy $3,000,000 limit and a $1,500,000 increase above the $4,500,000 figure initially proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement. For a qualifying CCPC, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out strictly on the basis of the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the claimant corporation and all of its associated corporations.

Under the enacted phase-out boundaries, a qualifying CCPC retains the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit when its combined taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year is $15,000,000 or less (increased from the legacy $10,000,000 lower threshold). Between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit shrinks on a straight-line basis, reaching zero once combined prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 or more (increased from the legacy $50,000,000 upper boundary). Mathematically, for a full 365-day taxation year, the annual SR&ED Expenditure Limit is governed by the linear reduction equation:

where A denotes the amount (not exceeding $60,000,000) by which the combined prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporate group exceeds $15,000,000. Under this slope, every $10.00 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the corporation's $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1.00.

For eligible Canadian public corporations, applying a balance-sheet taxable capital test would have prematurely disqualified research-intensive public companies that raise substantial share capital on public markets before generating significant commercial revenue. Accordingly, the enacted legislation applies the exact same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 straight-line phase-out formula to eligible Canadian public corporations, but measures the reduction on the corporation's (and its associated group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding taxation years rather than taxable capital.

body.text: 3.3 The General 15% Credit Rate and Refundability Matrix

All qualified SR&ED expenditures that do not qualify for the 35% enhanced rate—specifically, qualified spending by a qualifying CCPC or eligible Canadian public corporation in excess of its annual expenditure limit, as well as all qualified spending by foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, and large enterprises whose prior-year taxable capital or three-year average revenue is $75,000,000 or more—earn the general SR&ED ITC rate of 15%.

For corporate treasury management, the distinction between a refundable and a non-refundable ITC is critical. A refundable ITC is paid out in cash by the CRA to the extent that the credit exceeds the taxpayer's federal tax otherwise payable, providing immediate non-dilutive working capital even when the company is in a tax-loss position. Conversely, a non-refundable ITC only lowers federal Part I tax payable; if the corporation owes no federal income tax in the current year, the unused credit is retained and applied against federal tax payable in another taxation year. Under section 127.1 of the ITA, refundability varies systematically across taxpayer categories and between current expenditures and restored capital expenditures:

body.text: 3.4 Associated Corporation Allocation and Short Taxation Year Proration

Two mandatory anti-avoidance and proration mechanics govern the application of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit across corporate groups and fiscal periods. First, where a claimant corporation is associated with one or more other corporations within the meaning of the ITA (for example, where an individual or parent company owns or controls more than one corporation), the entire associated group must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit among its members, and the prior-year taxable capital (or three-year average gross revenue) of all associated companies is combined when calculating the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out reduction. Second, if a corporation has a short taxation year—defined as a fiscal period of fewer than 51 weeks, which frequently arises upon incorporation, amalgamation, or a change of control—its annual expenditure limit is reduced in strict proportion to the number of days in the short taxation year divided by 365.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Elections, and Capital Restoration
4.1 Domestic and Foreign Salaries and Wages

Employee salaries and wages typically represent the largest expenditure component of a Canadian SR&ED claim. Under subsection 37(1) and clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) of the ITA, a claimant may include the portion of an employee's salary or wages (including employer contributions to CPP, EI, and benefits for hands-on SR&ED staff) that corresponds to the percentage of working time the individual spent directly engaged in performing, supervising, or supporting eligible SR&ED activities. For example, if a software developer, tester, or systems analyst spends 40% of their working time in the taxation year on eligible SR&ED work, 40% of their eligible salary counts toward the claim.

While SR&ED must generally be carried out within Canada, subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA (claimed on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661 for work performed after February 25, 2008) permits a claimant to earn SR&ED deductions and ITCs on salaries or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada, provided four statutory conditions are satisfied. Specifically, the work outside Canada must be performed directly by an employee of the claimant (foreign contractor expenses are strictly ineligible); the employee must be resident in Canada and not subject to income or profits tax on that remuneration by another country; the foreign activities must be an integral part of the SR&ED activities performed in Canada by the claimant; and the total eligible foreign SR&ED salaries or wages claimed in the taxation year cannot exceed 10% of the total eligible salaries or wages for SR&ED performed in Canada by the claimant in that year. Notably, permissible foreign SR&ED wages reported on Lines 307 and 309 within this 10% ceiling also qualify for inclusion in the salary base when computing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Part 5 of Form T661.

In addition, tax auditors strictly verify compliance with the 180-day unpaid remuneration rule. Any salary or wages accrued as an expense in a taxation year that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of that taxation year cannot be claimed in the year accrued; instead, they may only be claimed on Line 310 of Form T661 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid, and such prior-year unpaid wages are permanently excluded from the PPA salary base under the proxy method.
4.2 Specified Employees and Regulation 2900 Salary Base Restrictions

Special statutory restrictions apply to "specified employees", defined as any employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation (or a related corporation). Because startup founders, owner-managers, and family-enterprise principals almost invariably meet this definition, structuring their compensation is a pivotal SR&ED compliance task. First, founders who pay themselves exclusively via dividends rather than employment salary generate zero eligible SR&ED wage expenditures and add nothing to the PPA salary base. Second, for specified employees compensated via salary, all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are excluded, and their maximum claimable direct SR&ED salary is capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for Canada Pension Plan purposes.

Third, when the claimant elects the Proxy Method, subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9) of the ITR impose an additional, tighter ceiling on the amount of a specified employee's salary that can enter the salary base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. After Regulation 2900(9) excludes bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages for every employee, Regulation 2900(7) restricts the maximum amount included in the PPA salary base for a specified employee to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary or wages (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, net of excluded items) or 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee):

In this statutory formula, A is the CPP YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days employed in the taxation year. For the 2026 taxation year, 2.5 × A equals $186,500, meaning an owner-manager employed for the full year counts at most the lesser of 75% of salary and $186,500 in the proxy salary base. Furthermore, under Regulation 2900(8), if the same specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, those associated corporations must share a single ceiling across the entire associated group.
4.3 Overhead Elections: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

When filing an SR&ED claim, a taxpayer must elect on Line 160 of Form T661 between two mutually exclusive methods for claiming SR&ED overhead: the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR). Pursuant to subsection 37(10) of the ITA, this election must be made on the first Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is locked and irrevocable for that taxation year once filed.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not track or claim actual overhead or indirect support expenditures; instead, it computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED. The PPA earns the 35% or 15% ITC under subsection 127(9) (though it is not added to the section 37 deduction pool) and shields the claimant from having to prove incremental utility usage or clerical time during a CRA audit. However, claimants must always test Regulation 2900(6) before electing the proxy method: Regulation 2900(6) imposes an overall cap on the PPA, stipulating that the PPA cannot exceed the corporation's total business deductions for the year less specified deductions (including direct SR&ED costs and building rent). A startup whose total expenses consist almost entirely of direct SR&ED salaries and building rent can see its PPA capped well below 55% under Regulation 2900(6).

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant tracks and claims actual overhead expenditures that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED (Paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the ITR) or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED (Paragraph 2900(3)(b) of the ITR). To illustrate the quantitative trade-off between the two methods, consider a qualifying CCPC well under the $6,000,000 expenditure limit with a December 31, 2026 year-end whose non-specified employees earned $300,000 for hands-on SR&ED work (with no bonuses), whose owner-manager (a specified shareholder) earned $200,000 and spent 80% of the year ($160,000) on hands-on SR&ED, and which incurred $30,000 of consumed materials and $150,000 of provable, directly related, incremental overhead. Under the Proxy Method, the non-specified employees contribute $300,000 to the salary base, while the owner-manager's $160,000 SR&ED salary is capped by Regulation 2900(7) at $150,000 (the lesser of 75% × $200,000 = $150,000 and the 2026 ceiling of $186,500), yielding a total PPA salary base of $450,000 and a 55% PPA of $247,500. Because the $247,500 PPA exceeds the $150,000 of actual incremental overhead, the Proxy Method generates a larger ITC (though the Traditional Method leaves $150,000 more inside the deductible section 37 pool because neither the PPA nor the overhead it replaces enters the section 37 pool under the proxy method).

body.text: 4.4 Materials Consumed or Transformed and Cloud Computing Infrastructure

Under both the Traditional Method (Paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR) and the Proxy Method (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA), a claimant may claim the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass physical supplies destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials, whereas materials transformed encompass raw materials and components integrated into experimental prototypes, pilot plants, or test batches during systematic investigation (excluding materials incorporated into commercial products sold without triggering ITC recapture). To substantiate material costs on audit, claimants must retain purchase invoices and contemporaneous usage logs tying each material batch directly to an eligible experimental build.

For software, artificial intelligence, and digital engineering enterprises, cloud computing costs (such as AWS, Google Cloud Platform [GCP], and Microsoft Azure elastic compute instances used directly for SR&ED experimentation and model training) require careful classification. While dedicated cloud computing environments used exclusively for SR&ED testing and experimentation are recognized as eligible SR&ED costs when segregated from commercial production hosting, the claimant's overhead election on Line 160 of Form T661 is decisive. Specifically, if a studio or software firm elects the Proxy Method, general software subscriptions and overhead hosting are already represented by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4), meaning that claiming such subscriptions separately would constitute impermissible double-claiming.
4.5 Arm's-Length Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Performers, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts out eligible SR&ED work to an arm's-length subcontractor to be performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the contract expenditure enters the section 37 deduction pool, while subsection 127(9) of the ITA includes 80% of the eligible contract payment as a qualified expenditure for ITC calculation purposes. To defend subcontractor claims during a CRA review, the claimant must provide statements of work and itemized invoices identifying the specific eligible SR&ED activities performed in Canada. Moreover, under the contract-SR&ED and third-party SR&ED rules in the ITA, the qualified expenditures of a Canadian contractor performing SR&ED on behalf of a payer are statutorily reduced by the contract amount under subsection 127(18) so that both parties cannot claim the ITC on the same expenditure.

For third-party payments—such as payments made to approved universities, research institutes, or agricultural organizations for SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business—the same 80% ITC inclusion rate applies. Notably, agricultural producers making contributions to agricultural organizations for SR&ED are exempted from completing Form T661 for those contributions and instead report them directly on Schedule 31, Part 8, Line 350. Where SR&ED expenditures are transferred between related (non-arm's-length) parties, the transferor and transferee must execute a written agreement accompanying Form T661 to substantiate the "transferred to" and "transferred from" qualified expenditure amounts.
4.6 Restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures and the Productivity Super-Deduction

A cornerstone of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the August 15, 2025 draft legislation, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) is the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 and becoming available for use on or after that date. Under the restored capital rules, depreciable property that is used all or substantially all for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—including specialized laboratory and engineering equipment, custom tooling, moulds, and outright-purchased computers and software—qualifies once again for both the section 37 deduction pool and the section 127 ITC. For a qualifying CCPC or eligible Canadian public corporation claiming within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the 35% enhanced ITC earned on restored capital expenditures is 40% refundable in cash (yielding a 14.0% cash refund and a 21.0% non-refundable tax credit). However, three strict capital exclusions remain in force: land and buildings are permanently excluded from SR&ED; general office equipment and furniture cannot be claimed when electing the Proxy Method; and equipment lease payments (which were excluded in 2014) were not restored by Bill C-15.

In tandem with the SR&ED capital restoration, Federal Budget 2025 introduced a "Productivity Super-Deduction" providing temporary immediate expensing (a 100% deduction in the first taxation year) for the cost of eligible manufacturing or processing buildings (including eligible additions or alterations) where at least 90% of the building's floor space is used to manufacture or process goods. Used property qualifies only if neither the taxpayer nor a non-arm's-length person previously owned the building and it was not acquired on a tax-deferred rollover basis, and recapture rules apply if the building's use subsequently changes. This 100% immediate write-off applies to eligible buildings acquired on or after Budget Day 2025 and first used for manufacturing or processing before 2030, phasing down to an enhanced first-year CCA rate of 75% for property first used in 2030 or 2031, and 55% for property first used in 2032 or 2033, with no enhanced rate available after 2033. Additionally, taxpayers financing capital and R&D operations must account for the Excessive Interest and Financing Expenses Limitation (EIFEL) rules (which apply a 30% fixed ratio of adjusted taxable income for taxation years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, following a 40% transitional ratio), as well as the Budget 2024 and August 15, 2025 proposals to expand "exempt interest and financing expenses (IFE)".
5. Technical Eligibility Criteria, Jurisprudence, and Audit Defence
5.1 The CRA's Two-Requirement Framework ("The Why" and "The How")

To establish a unified, accessible framework for claimants and CRA officials, the CRA replaced its archived Eligibility of Work policy and Information Circular IC 86-4R3 with the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The CRA emphasizes that both the judicial five-question test and the administrative Two Requirements ("The Why" and "The How") derive directly from the unchanged statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

Under the CRA's administrative guidelines, Requirement 1 ("The Why") mandates that the work be undertaken for the purpose of advancing scientific knowledge or achieving a technological advancement. A systematic investigation is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning that it cannot be determined whether a given technical objective or result can be achieved, or how to achieve it, based on available scientific or technological knowledge. Crucially, the CRA measures the baseline of available knowledge against the combined scientific or technological knowledge of the resources within the claimant's business. If a technical team encounters a problem and simply circumvents it with a workaround using available knowledge and standard practice, the CRA guidelines specify that the work is ineligible; the underlying technological uncertainty must actually be investigated rather than sidestepped.

Simultaneously, Requirement 2 ("The How") mandates that the work be executed as a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals. Random trial-and-error or unguided attempts until a configuration works fail Requirement 2. Instead, the CRA requires a structured scientific process in which the claimant formulates a clear hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point, tests that hypothesis by means of controlled experiments or analysis, develops logical conclusions based on the empirical results, and generates contemporaneous evidence as the work progresses. Because the CRA's two requirements evaluate the purpose of the work and how it was conducted rather than commercial success, a failed project or disproven hypothesis fully qualifies for SR&ED, and documented technical failures often serve as compelling evidence that the outcome was genuinely uncertain at the outset.
5.2 Foundational Jurisprudence: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants and the Five Questions

The foundational judicial authority interpreting subsection 248(1) of the ITA is the 1998 decision of Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (T.C.C.). Referring to Information Circular IC 86-4R3 as a generally useful analytical framework, Chief Justice Bowman articulated the classic five questions that Canadian courts and CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) apply to determine whether a project constitutes eligible SR&ED.

First, the court asks whether there was a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures—that is, techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. As Chief Justice Bowman observed, technological uncertainty is something that exists in the mind of the specialist when routine engineering cannot predictably resolve the problem. Second, the court examines whether the person claiming SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the systematic formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through experiment or analysis. Fourth, the court determines whether the process was undertaken for the purpose of resulting in a scientific or technological advancement. Fifth, the court verifies whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, the procedures adopted, and the results was maintained as the work progressed.
5.3 Evidentiary Standards and Contemporaneous Documentation: R I S - Christie Ltd. and 6379249 Canada Inc.

While Northwest Hydraulic established the substantive five-question framework, the Federal Court of Appeal decision in R I S - Christie Ltd. v. Canada (also cited as R I S - Christie Ltd. v. The Queen), 1998 CanLII 8876 (FCA), 99 D.T.C. 5087, FCA Docket A-710-96 (rendered December 21, 1998) defines the governing evidentiary standard for proving systematic investigation and repeatability. Writing for the Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Robertson held that because scientific research and experimental development requires systematic testing and repeatability, a claimant must produce objective documentary evidence of its experimental tests and results rather than merely asserting through retrospective oral testimony that SR&ED was performed. The CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors expressly cites R I S - Christie Ltd. v. Canada to instruct RTAs on the legal distinction between a taxpayer merely asserting that work was SR&ED and actually proving it to be SR&ED through contemporaneous records.

Similarly, in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015, TCC Docket 2012-3634), the Tax Court of Canada applied Chief Justice Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic criteria under subsection 248(1) while simultaneously enforcing the strict statutory time limits for filing prescribed information on Form T661 under subsection 37(11) of the ITA. Collectively, these rulings establish that surviving a CRA technical and financial review requires both a valid technological uncertainty and contemporaneous experimental records generated as the work progresses—such as design of experiments, laboratory notebooks, source-code commit histories, ticket logs, and quantitative test benchmarks.

body.text: 5.4 Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, and Product Design Eligibility Nuances

Because the CRA maintains no separate software-specific guidance, software development, cloud computing architectures, artificial intelligence, and industrial product design are evaluated under the same universal subsection 248(1) criteria as traditional physical sciences. In both software engineering and product design studios, the most common reason claims are disallowed is that the claimant describes a business problem or commercial objective (such as "we needed to build a faster data processing system for our customers") rather than a technological uncertainty. Routine feature work, standard API integrations, and routine design iterations do not qualify for SR&ED regardless of how many hours they absorb. Conversely, when engineers or software developers identify specific technological barriers inside their projects that existing design methods and standard practice cannot resolve—and document their hypotheses, abstract syntax tree (AST) deltas, [commit:file:line] code citations, prototype builds, blind alleys, and test results—those specific slices of engineering investigation qualify.
6. Governing Authorities, Filing Procedures, Form T661 Architecture, and Deadlines
6.1 Institutional Roles of the Canada Revenue Agency and Department of Finance Canada

The administration of Canada's federal R&D tax incentive system is divided between two federal institutions. The Department of Finance Canada formulates tax policy, conducts public consultations, models tax expenditures (using micro-simulation models and benchmark tax projections), and drafts legislative amendments to the ITA and ITR. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the SR&ED program on a day-to-day basis, deploying Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) to evaluate whether claimed projects satisfy the scientific and technological requirements of subsection 248(1) of the ITA and Financial Reviewers to audit expenditure pools, overhead elections, and ITC calculations under sections 37 and 127.
6.2 Structural Anatomy of Form T661 and Schedule 31

To claim federal SR&ED incentives, a corporation must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) (prepared in accordance with Guide T4088 and the CRA's SR&ED workbook) together with Schedule 31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) as part of its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. Because Form T661 incorporates electronic fields for all prescribed information, claimants transmitting their return via T2 Bar Codes or EFILE must not mail duplicate paper copies of Form T661 to the CRA. Furthermore, tax preparation software includes a print-suppression checkbox allowing a claimant to omit the confidential technical narratives on Lines 242, 244, and 246 when printing client/office copies or copies intended for Revenu Québec without affecting the electronic transmission to the CRA.

Form T661 is organized into ten parts, where the main form aggregates corporate-wide SR&ED figures for the fiscal year and Part 2 serves as a project-specific schedule completed once for each SR&ED project claimed:

body.text: 6.3 Technical Narrative Precision: Part 2 Section B (Lines 242, 244, and 246)

Part 2, Section B of Form T661 is the decisive technical component of an SR&ED claim where projects either succeed or fail during initial CRA screening. While a prior version of Form T661 included a separate Line 240 asking what technological advancements were sought (maximum 350 words), the current Form T661 Part 2 Section B structures the technical narrative into three tightly linked questions governed by strict 350 / 700 / 350 word limits.

On Line 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties — Maximum 350 Words), the claimant must describe the specific technological obstacles or uncertainties that had to be overcome, referencing quantitative technical metrics, system constraints, or performance thresholds and explaining why existing knowledge, standard engineering practice, or documented tools were insufficient. On Line 244 (Work Performed in the Tax Year / Systematic Investigation — Maximum 700 Words), the claimant must summarize the systematic investigation performed in the taxation year to overcome the uncertainties described in Line 242, detailing the specific hypotheses formulated, the controlled experiments, prototypes, or analyses conducted to test those hypotheses, the technical failures, blind alleys, and re-dos encountered, the empirical metrics measured, and the conclusions drawn. On Line 246 (Scientific or Technological Advancements Achieved — Maximum 350 Words), the claimant must articulate the specific new scientific or technological knowledge gained as a result of the work described in Line 244, connecting that new knowledge directly back to the uncertainty defined in Line 242.

Guide T4088 emphasizes that personnel directly familiar with the scientific or technical content of the work should draft Part 2 Section B in clear, concise technical language. Furthermore, on the financial lines of Form T661, claimants should always enter exact dollar figures calculated from accounting ledgers for materials and subcontracts rather than rounded numbers, as rounded figures signal to CRA auditors that estimates were used and increase audit selection risk. For classified projects, Guide T4088 instructs the claimant to attach a copy of the official classification letter to its tax return and Form T661, omit the separate sheet containing the Part 2 Section B narratives from the submitted return, and retain a copy of the Section B information in its corporate records.
6.4 Part 9 Claim Preparer Disclosures and Statutory Penalty Provisions

Under the CRA's Filing Requirements Policy, Part 9 of Form T661 (Claim Preparer Information) must be completed in full to disclose each external claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim, together with the billing arrangement (such as contingency fee rates vs. flat/hourly fees). If the prescribed information regarding claim preparers and billing arrangements in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 statutory penalty may be assessed. Where a claim preparer prepared or assisted with the form, the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable for the $1,000 penalty. However, the CRA's policy explicitly confirms that an SR&ED claim will not be disallowed solely because information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate.
6.5 The Strict 18-Month Reporting Deadline and Subsection 220(2.2) Bar on Discretion

Under subsection 37(11) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the statutory reporting deadline for filing an SR&ED claim (Form T661 and Schedule 31 containing all prescribed information) is 12 months after the filing-due date of the income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation has a total of 18 months after the end of its taxation year to file its SR&ED claim. To illustrate, if a corporation's taxation year ends on December 31, 2025, its T2 corporate return is due on June 30, 2026, and its complete SR&ED claim for that taxation year must reach the CRA on or before June 30, 2027; on July 1, 2027, the SR&ED credit and deduction pool addition for that year are permanently lost.

Crucially, subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA bars the Minister of National Revenue from exercising discretionary fairness relief to extend the SR&ED reporting deadline. A corporation may file its T2 return on time at the 6-month mark and add the SR&ED claim by amendment up to the 18-month reporting deadline, but it must never confuse the 6-month T2 deadline with the 18-month SR&ED deadline, nor expect any extension past 18 months. Moreover, the CRA's Filing Requirements Policy distinguishes between failure to meet Schedule 31 ITC filing requirements (which forfeits the ITC while leaving allowable expenditures in the section 37 pool if T661 was timely filed) and failure to file prescribed Form T661 information by the 18-month deadline (which forfeits both the section 37 deduction and the section 127 ITC in their entirety).
6.6 CRA Review Workflows, Service Standards, and Pre-Claim Advisory Programs

For refundable SR&ED claims, the CRA's published service standard is 60 days if the claim is accepted as filed without audit, and 90 to 180 days if the claim is selected for a technical and financial review, with the processing clock starting only once the CRA has received both the complete SR&ED claim and the T2 return. To streamline processing, the CRA increasingly utilizes automated risk-assessment tools to route low-risk claims through without a manual audit, making early simultaneous filing of the T2 and T661 the fastest way to receive cash refunds.

To assist businesses before and after filing, the CRA provides three dedicated support services. First, the online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) helps taxpayers test whether their work meets the "Why" and "How" eligibility requirements before preparing a claim. Second, the Pre-Claim Consultation and Pre-Claim Approval program (available to applicants with gross business income below $25,000,000) offers upfront technical guidance prior to filing. Third, for businesses filing their first SR&ED claim (or that have not filed a claim in the preceding three years), the CRA selects claimants after filing for a virtual educational session; if selected by the CRA, participation is mandatory, though the session is an advisory walkthrough rather than an audit of the filed claim.
7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Stacking Mechanics
7.1 Government Assistance Grinding Mechanics Under Subsection 127(9)

Across Canada, provincial and territorial governments administer R&D tax credits that stack alongside the federal SR&ED program. Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, however, any provincial or territorial R&D tax credit (as well as any direct government grant) constitutes "government assistance" that reduces the taxpayer's federal pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures before the 35% or 15% federal ITC is calculated. Consequently, if a claimant incurs E dollars of eligible SR&ED expenditure, receives a provincial tax credit at effective rate p, and earns the federal ITC at rate f, the combined federal-provincial credit follows the net stacking relationship:
Combined credit = E × [p + f × (1 − p)]
By accounting for this government assistance reduction early in the claim preparation workflow, corporate tax teams ensure accurate federal ITC reporting on Part 4 of Form T661 and Schedule 31.
7.2 Québec: The 2025–2026 Overhaul, the New CRIC Regime, and the CDAEIA

In its 2025–2026 Budget unveiled on March 25, 2025, the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive restructuring of its provincial R&D and innovation tax incentives for taxation years (and partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025. To consolidate tax assistance and eliminate less effective measures, Québec abolished six legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025: the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (which had previously offered up to 30% subject to a $50 million–$75 million consolidated asset threshold); the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium; the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research; the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium; the Tax Credit for In-House Design Activities (Industrial Design); and the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services. In addition, Québec abolished the five-year personal income tax holidays for foreign researchers and foreign experts effective March 26, 2025.

In place of the six abolished R&D tax credits, Québec introduced the consolidated, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation), administered by Revenu Québec and claimed by attaching Form RD-1029.8.CR-T to the Québec corporate income tax return for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. To qualify for the CRIC, a corporation must operate a business in Québec, maintain an establishment there, and undertake (or cause to be undertaken on its behalf under contract) eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec. Unlike the abolished R&D wage credit, CRIC credit rates are based strictly on a corporation's volume of eligible spending rather than its asset size, granting every eligible corporation (and shared across associated corporate groups, though excluding partnership allocations from the higher tier) a 30% refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the annual exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable tax credit on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier.

Crucially, the CRIC expands both the scope of eligible activities and the eligible cost base in Québec. Alongside basic research, applied research, and experimental development (including incremental improvements), the CRIC newly covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec—specifically: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and obtain an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; and (2) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials. Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization in Québec, 50% of amounts paid to an arm's-length subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity (for which the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue recognition certificates), and 100% of property (equipment) acquisition costs in Québec (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property used under a large investment project tax holiday certificate). To earn the CRIC, a corporation's qualified expenditures in the taxation year must exceed its applicable exclusion threshold, which is defined as the greater of $50,000 or the sum across all eligible employees of the basic personal amount under the Québec personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025) adjusted in proportion to the time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

Alongside the CRIC, Québec reformed its e-business tax credit for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025 into the Development of E-Business Tax Credit Integrating Artificial Intelligence (CDAEIA), administered jointly by Investissement Québec (which issues mandatory annual eligibility certificates verifying activity, service, and minimum employment criteria) and Revenu Québec. The CDAEIA refocuses tax assistance on IT corporations that meaningfully integrate artificial intelligence (AI) functionalities, newly includes data processing and hosting activities to facilitate AI company eligibility, and excludes routine maintenance or scaling activities. The total CDAEIA credit rate is up to 30%, with the non-refundable portion increasing by 1% per year until reaching 10% non-refundable and 20% refundable in 2028; however, both the refundable and non-refundable CDAEIA rates are halved for any taxation year in which at least 50% of the corporation's gross revenue is derived from inter-company outsourcing of applications developed for use exclusively outside Québec by a related / non-arm's-length ultimate beneficiary. Complementary Québec innovation incentives include the Investment and Innovation Tax Credit (IITC) (up to 25% of eligible project costs, paired with the 2025–2026 Budget's reinstatement of a 100% immediate depreciation rate through 2029 for manufacturing and processing machinery, clean energy equipment, and zero-emission vehicles), the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) (offering a reduced Québec tax rate via a deduction of up to 83%), and the Tax Credit for External Design in Québec (up to 24% for external fashion design activities).
7.3 Ontario: The OITC, ORDTC, and Co-operative Education Incentives

In Ontario, corporate R&D tax credits are established by the Ontario Ministry of Finance (Government of Ontario) and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through the T2 corporate return. The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides a refundable tax credit of up to 8% on eligible R&D expenditures in Ontario for small and medium-sized corporations. Stacking alongside the OITC and federal SR&ED is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), a non-refundable tax credit that provides additional Ontario corporate tax relief on eligible SR&ED spending and reduces provincial tax payable. Furthermore, Ontario businesses that hire post-secondary co-op students from approved Ontario institutions can claim the Ontario Co-operative Education Tax Credit (OCELC)—administered via the CRA on Schedule 550 / Form ON479—which provides a 25% to 30% refundable tax credit up to a maximum of $3,000 per student placement.
7.4 British Columbia, Alberta, Yukon, and Manitoba Innovation Incentives

Across Western and Northern Canada, several targeted provincial and territorial tax credits stack with the federal SR&ED regime. In British Columbia, corporations performing SR&ED in the province can claim the 10% British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit (which is 100% refundable for qualifying CCPCs and non-refundable for other corporations) by filing Form T666 within a strict statutory deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year. In Alberta, the provincial government administers the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), which provides a refundable grant/tax credit of 8% on base R&D spending and an enhanced rate (incorporating a 12% incremental rate) on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to a $4,000,000 annual spending limit, phasing out for corporations with taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000. In the Yukon, the Yukon R&D Tax Credit provides a 15% refundable tax credit on eligible R&D expenditures incurred in the territory. In Manitoba, Manitoba Finance (Tax Assistance Office) supports technical workforce integration through the Co-operative Students Hiring Incentive (COS-HI) (a 15% refundable tax credit on co-op student wages up to $5,000 per student across all work terms) and the Co-operative Graduate Hiring Incentive (COG-HI) (a 15% refundable tax credit on full-time co-op graduate wages up to $2,500 per year and $5,000 total per hire).

body.text: 8. Complementary Federal Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits and Strategic Conclusions
8.1 Integration with the Clean Economy Investment Tax Credit Suite and Sectoral Credits

To complement the SR&ED program and accelerate industrial capital formation, the federal government deployed five major Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits alongside targeted labour and cultural production incentives. While SR&ED funds experimental R&D, the Clean Economy ITCs—two of which, the Clean Electricity and Clean Technology ITCs, Federal Budget 2026 proposed extending to property that becomes available for use before 2041—provide substantial refundable capital subsidies during commercial deployment. Specifically, the Clean Technology Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit (CTM ITC) provides an up to 30% refundable tax credit on clean-tech manufacturing equipment investments covering solar, wind, batteries, electric vehicles, and critical minerals processing (open until December 31, 2034). The Clean Technology Investment Tax Credit provides an up to 30% refundable tax credit on clean tech capital investments (dropping to 20% without labour requirements and to 15% for property that becomes available for use in 2034). The Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit (CEITC)—enacted in March 2026 and retroactive to April 2024, administered by the CRA and Natural Resources Canada—provides a 15% refundable tax credit on eligible capital costs for clean electricity generation, storage, and transmission for for-profit businesses, Indigenous organizations, and public bodies through December 31, 2034. Furthermore, the Clean Hydrogen Investment Tax Credit provides a 15% to 40% refundable tax credit on clean hydrogen production equipment varying by carbon intensity (40% for carbon intensity below 0.75 kg of CO₂e per kg of hydrogen) through December 31, 2034, while the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage Investment Tax Credit (CCUS ITC) provides a 37.5% to 60% refundable tax credit on eligible CCUS equipment (60% for direct air capture) through December 31, 2040.

In addition to clean economy capital credits, Canadian enterprises frequently stack the Apprenticeship Job Creation Tax Credit (AJCTC)—a $2,000 non-refundable tax credit per apprentice per year for eligible wages in Red Seal trades during the first two years of apprenticeship—with their SR&ED claims. Similarly, digital media and production companies leverage the Canadian Film or Video Production Tax Credit (CPTC) (25% fully refundable credit on Canadian labour costs) and the Film or Video Production Services Tax Credit (PSTC) (16% refundable credit on Canadian labour spend, minimum $1M labour spend per project), both administered jointly by the Canadian Audio-Visual Certification Office (CAVCO) and the CRA.
8.2 Strategic Compliance and Optimization Conclusions for Canadian Claimants

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the retroactive doubling of the federal enhanced SR&ED expenditure limit to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, and the launch of Québec's CRIC and CDAEIA regimes require a proactive recalibration of corporate R&D tax governance across Canada. First, qualifying CCPCs and newly eligible Canadian public corporations must immediately review their fixed-asset additions on or after December 16, 2024 to capture restored SR&ED capital expenditures (including custom tooling, moulds, and dedicated R&D computing hardware used all or substantially all for SR&ED) while modelling the expanded $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital and three-year average revenue phase-out corridors. Second, founder-led enterprises must structure owner-manager compensation as T4 employment salary rather than dividends—targeting the Regulation 2900(7) PPA ceiling of $186,500 in 2026 and ensuring all accrued remuneration is paid within 180 days of year-end—while testing the Regulation 2900(6) PPA overall cap before locking in the irrevocable Line 160 overhead election on Form T661.

Third, corporations operating in Québec must transition their project accounting for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 from the six abolished legacy credits to the size-agnostic 30% / 20% refundable CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T), expanding internal time-tracking and capital tracking to capture newly eligible pre-commercialization regulatory validation tests and functional/aesthetic product design above the annual exclusion threshold. Fourth, to satisfy the strict evidentiary standards of Northwest Hydraulic Consultants and R I S - Christie Ltd. v. Canada, technical teams must generate contemporaneous records—linking hypotheses, experimental test logs, failed builds, and code commits directly to Form T661 Part 2 Lines 242, 244, and 246 within the strict 350 / 700 / 350 word gates—while enforcing absolute calendar controls over the non-extendable 18-month statutory filing deadline under subsections 37(11) and 220(2.2) of the ITA.
